excerpt_en: The **Nuija-Heikki väkikivi** in the village of Synsiö, Kangasniemi, is located a short distance northeast of the Vehkomäki farm, on a rocky outcrop that slopes toward the farm. According to popular tradition, Nuija-Heikki is said to have carried this stone from the bog on the farm side up onto the rock. The stone is 150 cm high on the western side and 75 cm on the eastern side, 125 cm long and 60 cm thick, and therefore cannot have been brought there by an ordinary carrying pole. On the side of the stone, some common man has indistinctly carved the name of the stone mentioned above.

excerpt_en:
4.5. Lifting stones (väkikiviä)?

Castrén (1886: 35–36) reports that in the kihlakunta of Haapajärvi, more specifically in the Pyhäjärvi area, so-called stone tables (kivipöydät) are referred to as väkikivet. According to Castrén, the terminology varies by region, and elsewhere the stones are described as giants’ lifting stones. The term is clarified in Sarkkinen (2010) in an inspection report on the eastern stone table of Kaakkomäki in Pyhäjärvi: a year after the inspection, Sarkkinen received information stating that the structure had been built in the 1940s, possibly as a demonstration of the builders’ strength. The structure is therefore likely a väkikivi.

The stone table in question differs from others in that it consists of a level ground stone serving as a base, upon which stand legs supporting a central stone, with a round capstone on top. Väkikivi thus appears to refer specifically to stone tables constructed expressly for the purpose of lifting stones.

The stone table described by Castrén between the Haukilampi lakes is located approximately 2.5 km southwest of the stone inspected by Sarkkinen. The Haukilampi structure likewise has small stones set upon a large ground stone, with a flat stone on top. Could this represent a local tradition that was later forgotten? Castrén (1886: 38–42) notes that there are numerous other stone tables south and northeast of Pyhäjärvi, many of them in the same area as the Kaakkomäki east and Haukilampi stone tables. Castrén himself, however, doubts that most of the stone tables are man-made. One of his alternative interpretations is that the stone tables of the Haapajärvi kihlakunta might have been constructed by topographers during their survey expeditions; yet he questions this as well, believing that the local population would have noticed if stone tables had suddenly appeared in the forest.

The väkikivi tradition is not confined solely to the Pyhäjärvi region. Paasonen (1889: 146) describes two stone tables in the kihlakunta of Mikkeli that are undoubtedly väkikivet. According to Paasonen, the smooth surface of the Nuija-Heikki väkikivi bears the inscription: “TÄ_ON NVIH?IF?I VÄ KIVI”. He further notes that another similar stone in the kihlakunta carries the inscription: “Otto Aatunpojan väkikivi”. These stones are apparently the only stone tables that bear inscriptions or any traces of working at all. The dating of the väkikivet is unknown, but they are presumably relatively late constructions.

Can the väkikivi interpretation be applied to other stone tables in the material? The Pyhäjärvi stone tables differ structurally from others, but the stones mentioned by Castrén may resemble those in the remainder of the material. The inscribed stones, for their part, appear to be structurally similar to other stone tables; at least the Nuija-Heikki väkikivi is situated on bare rock (Paasonen 1889: 146). Stone tables may thus have been constructed without any particular purpose. In such cases, their true nature is unlikely ever to be revealed.

Source cited: Paasonen 1889: p. 146 (Paasonen, Julius 1889. Muinaisjäännöksiä ja -muistoja Mikkelin kihlakunnassa).

excerpt_fi: Hankasalmeen lohenneitten pitäjäläisten kanssa on waan kowat riidat kassain jakamisesta, sillä he tekewät niin tarkkaa, että kirkosta ynnä pappilan wirkataloista tahtowat osia. Ruiskaswit yleisesti huonon-puoleiset, waan suwi-touon oraat wähän paremmat. Heinät lupaawat hywää satoa. C. lämpömittari on päiwässä osottanut tänään 38½ ja yöllä 20½ astetta. Eihän silloin enään turkkia tarwita. Historiallisia wanhoja nimiä täällä löytyy 2 Hiidennientä, Hiidenluola, Hiislammin kangas, Lappi, Lapinpaasi, Käräjäniemi, Toranlahti, Pirttilahti ja -mäki, Terwamäki, Wawessaari, Lapinsalo, Ison Heikin wäkikiwi ja kalliokirjoitus Synsiön rannalla, Kerinkanta, Simpiö, Salwuri j. n. e.
excerpt_en:
Among the parishioners who have broken away to Hankasalmi, there are indeed fierce disputes over the division of parish funds, for they are so exacting that they demand shares even from the church itself and from the vicarage crown estates. The rye crops are generally on the poor side, but the summer grain seedlings are somewhat better. The hay meadows promise a good yield. The Celsius thermometer during the day has today shown 38½ degrees, and at night 20½ degrees. In such weather, a fur coat is no longer needed.

Old historical names are found here, including two places called Hiidenniemi, Hiidenluola, Hiislammin kangas, Lappi, Lapinpaasi, Käräjäniemi, Toranlahti, Pirttilahti and Pirttimäki, Tervamäki, Wawessaari, Lapinsalo, Ison Heikin väkikivi, and a rock carving on the shore of Synsiö, as well as Kerinkanta, Simpiö, Salwuri, and so forth.
note: Names 'Ison Heikin väkikivi' on the Synsiö shore; may be the same stone as Nuija-Heikin väkikivi.

excerpt_fi:
Nostokiwiä -
Myytävän kestikievaritalosta

Ritolan isäntä on myös kova hiihtäjä ja on ensimäisen palkinnon ottaja ensimäisissä Haapaveden hiihtokilpailuissa noin 30 vuotta takaperin, sitäpaitsi on hän innokas urheilun harrastaja. Eipä Ritolasta vieras juuri päässyt, ennenkuin oli talon isännän kanssa »kissanhäntää» vetänyt, väkikiveä nostanut t. m. s.
Ukolla on lisäksi verraton supliikki ja muisti, että kyllä hänellä juttelemista piisaa (liekö sitten kaikki juttunsa tosia), ja jos sattuisi maanpäälliset asiat loppumaan niin riittää ukolla omia ajatuksia tulevaisiin maailmoihinkin — vaan melkeinpä mieluisimmat puheenaineet ovat hänestä urheilua ja urheilijoita koskettelevat. Ukon tarkassa muistissa on muotiurheilun ennätyksiäkin — eikä ainoastaan hiihtohommiin kuuluvia. Tuntuupa monasti että tuossa syrjäisessä sydänmaan talossa harrastetaan ja toimitaan enemmän urheilun hyväksi, kuin monen varakkaan liikekeskuksissa asuvan urheilunharrastajan luona. Lämmin kädenlyönti lujakouraiselle Ukko Ritolalle.
excerpt_en:
The master of the Ritola farm is also a formidable skier and was the winner of the first prize in the very first Haapavesi skiing competitions some thirty years ago; in addition, he is an ardent devotee of sport. A visitor scarcely managed to leave Ritola before having pulled “the cat’s tail” with the master of the house, lifted a väkikivi, or engaged in the like.

The old man also possesses an incomparable gift of the gab and a remarkable memory, so that he never lacks for stories (whether all of them are true is another matter); and should earthly matters happen to run out, he has thoughts of his own enough for worlds to come as well—yet almost his favorite topics of conversation are those touching upon sport and sportsmen. In his precise memory reside records of fashionable sports too—and not only those related to skiing. It often seems that in that remote backwoods homestead more is done and pursued for the benefit of sport than in the homes of many a wealthy sports enthusiast living in commercial centers. A warm handshake to stout-fisted Old Man Ritola.

excerpt_fi:
Paavo ei ollut yksinäisyydessä elävä murjottuja, jollaiseksi hänet olisi luullut kasvoista katsoen, vaan oikea harrastusten mies. Hänellä oli useampia tuttavia kuin monella kauniimmalla, sillä jokainen tiesi että minkä asian Paavo ottaa ajaakseen, sitä ei keskeytä muu kuin kuolema tai lavantauti. Mutta Paavo ei ottanutkaan harrastaakseen yhtäaikaa kaiken maailman asioita. Yksi asia kerrallaan ja lujasti, se oli hänen työjärjestyksensä.
Nuoruuden ikäkaudella, jolloin muut katselevat itselleen elämänkumppania, oli Paavo saanut väkikiven nostoharrastuksen. Sitä ei kestänyt monta vuotta, mutta niin kokonaan se piti vallassaan, ettei hän tullut katsoneeksikaan hameväkeen päin. Paavon huomio oli niinä vuosina kääntynyt vankimman näköisiin miehiin, ja niiden täytyi olla peräti välinpitämättömiä voimainsa suuruudesta, jos eivät suostuneet väkikiven nostoon.
excerpt_en:
Paavo was not a sulking recluse, as one might have assumed from his appearance, but a true man of pursuits. He had more acquaintances than many a more handsome fellow, for everyone knew that whatever cause Paavo took upon himself, nothing would interrupt it except death or typhoid fever. Yet Paavo did not set out to pursue all manner of things at once. One thing at a time, and with determination—that was his order of work.

In his youthful years, when others are looking for a life companion, Paavo had taken up the pursuit of lifting väkikivi. It did not last many years, but it held him so completely in its grip that he did not so much as glance toward the womenfolk. During those years Paavo’s attention was turned toward the men who appeared the strongest, and they had to be utterly indifferent to the magnitude of their own strength if they refused to take part in lifting the väkikivi.

excerpt_fi: Entisajan voima' miehiä Ähtarissa. Jo „ryssänkesän" ajoilta v. 1808 on kansan keskuudessa Ähtärissä säilynyt erään voimamiehen muisto. Tapaninmäen talossa Hankaveden kylässä olivat ryssät koettaneet kivenmukuloilla särkeä ovea erääseen aittaan, jossa he luulivat olevan joitakin ruokatavaroita. Silloin muuan sen talon pojista otti ison louhukiven ja heitti sen aitan oveen, jotta ovi lensi aitan peräseinään. Kai ryssiä rupesi mokoma voimannäyte pelottamaan, koska he siinä paikassa lähtivät Tapaninmäestä. Tässä ryssistä puheen ollessa sopinee mainita ähtäriläisen miehen voimannäyte myös siltä ajalta, jolloin täällä oli kasakoita majoitettuina muka järjestyksen pitoa varten. Niitä oli vielä Aleksanteri ll:sen aikoina Ähtärissäkin, iiankolan talossa he kerran rupesivat vetämään väkikapulaa „Ison- Sampan" kanssa. Samppa oli verraton väkikapulan vetäjä, silla a.nä kasakan takapuoli nousi, kua Samppa veti. Siten kävi joka miehen kasakkain joukosta. Kovasti pulittaen he viimein lähtivät joukolla tiehensä, jotta Samppa jäi yksin voittajana paikalle. Mutta Samppa olikin väkevä mies. Hän kyllä nosti olkimitan (nuorissa) reestä ja kantoi sitä. Mutta Pohjos-Topiia Myllymäen läheltä vasta oli mies väkikalikan vedossa. Kerrankin hän voitti siinä urheilussa viisi miestä, jotka saivat joukolla olla häntä yhtä vastaan. Palkinnoksi sai hän silloin Tenhusen isännältä jommoisenkin määrän rukiii-i. tfe olivatkin Topiialle hyvään tarpeeseen, sillä silloin oli kova aika maassa. Toisena voimanäytteenä Pohjos-Topiiasta kerrotaan, että hän jokseenkin vain sormikoukullaan veti ison kirkkoveneen maihin. Vanha Siltalainen oli muuten hyvä hyppääjä, sillä hän hyppäsi tasakäpälää yhdeksästäkin tervatynnyrin kehästä, jotka olivat asetetut vierekkäin. Tämän poika Siltalan Kustavi nuorena taas oli voimamies. Kyläkunnan miesten väkikivi oli jossakin aidan vieressä, ja oli se niin raskas tavallisille miehille, ittä vain kaksi miestä koko kyläkunnasta jaksoi sitä hieman liikutella. Kun Kustavi kulki kerran siitä paikasta sivuitse, uin hän heitti kyläkunnan miesten väkikiven aidan taakse. Pahana olivat miehet pitäneet, kun olivat kuulleet Siltalan Kustavin voimateosta. Nämä jutut ovat niiltä ajoilta, jolloin ei vielä ollut järjestettyjä urheilukilpailuja pistemääräyksineen. Mutta voimainmittelyä ja muuta sukkeluuden näyttöä täytyi silloinkin olla. Yhteen tultua vedettiin väkikalikkaa, nostettiin väkikiveä, painiskeltiin, hyppäiltiin Monipuolinen oli »ohjelma" silloinkin. Yksinpä kirkkomatkoillakin syntyi eri venekuntain kesken kilpailua soudossa, jolloin isot kirkkoveneet liikkuivat laineilla, että kohisi vain. Kasvukeskisillä oli kiekonheittoa, pilpunheittoa, kolopiilosilla oloa, kilpajuoksua, hiibtoa y.m. Nuoret voimat siihenkin aikaan pursuivat runsauttaan ja vaativat käyttöään elämän kilpakentällä yli senkin, mitä niitä tarvittiin leivän saantia tarkoittavassa työssä. (Vaasassa -n)
excerpt_en:
His son, Kustavi of Siltala, in his youth, was in turn a strongman. The village men’s väkikivi stood somewhere by a fence, and it was so heavy for ordinary men that only two men in the entire village were able to move it even slightly. When Kustavi once passed by that spot, he threw the village men’s väkikivi over the fence. The men took it badly when they heard of Siltala Kustavi’s feat of strength.

These stories date from a time when there were not yet organized sporting competitions with point systems. Yet there had to be contests of strength and other displays of agility even then. When people gathered together, they pulled the väkikalikka, lifted the väkikivi, wrestled, and jumped. Versatile was the “programme” even in those days. Even on church journeys competition arose between different boat crews in rowing, when the large church boats cut through the waves with a roar. Among the youth there was discus throwing, peg throwing, hide-and-seek in tree hollows, foot races, sliding, and so forth. Young strength even then overflowed in abundance and demanded its use on life’s field of contest beyond what was required merely for the work of earning one’s bread.

En lyftesten
Ovan avbildade sten befinner sig i Nedervetil vid det vägskäl, där körvägen upp till Klockarbacken viker av från allmänna landsvägen och närmare bestämt på södra sidan av landsvägen. Stenen bär av gammalt namnet *Tomasasstäinä« (Tomas' sten). Den är välbekant för de manliga församlingsmedlemmarna i Nedervetil, ty varje år pröva skriftskolpojkarna sina krafter på densamma. Den, som orkar lyfta stenen från marken, betraktas av sina kamrater som fullvuxen, medan den, som icke mäktar med stenen, anses hava kommit för tidigt till skriftskolan. Och det måste nog erkännas, att den nutida skriftskolungdomen icke fyller måttet, ty en årgång skriftskolpojkar kan vanligen uppvisa endast ett par unga män, som lyfta stenen från marken. 1 De älsta nedervetilborna berätta, att «Tomasasstäinä« har varit föremål för skriftskolungdomens intresse redan före deras tid. Dessutom förklara de alla, att stenen har sitt namn av en man, som hette Tomas och bodde helt nära kyrkan, nämligen på Måsabacka. Denne Tomas skall hava burit stenen den 3 4 km. långa vägen från kyrkan till dess nuvarande plats. Om detta är sant, kan man föreställa sig, att han har vilat flere gånger på vägen. De, som berätta om sambandet iriellan Tomas och stenen, veta i allmänhet icke, när han levde. En person har dock lämnat uppgiften, att Tomas föddes omkr. år 1800.

excerpt_en:
A lifting stone

The stone depicted above is located in Nedervetil, at the road junction where the cart road leading up to Klockarbacken branches off from the public highway—more precisely, on the southern side of the highway. From olden times the stone has borne the name Tomasasstäinä (“Tomas’s stone”). It is well known to the male members of the parish in Nedervetil, for every year the confirmation-school boys test their strength on it. He who manages to lift the stone from the ground is regarded by his companions as full-grown, whereas he who cannot cope with the stone is considered to have come too early to confirmation school. And it must indeed be admitted that today’s confirmation-school youth does not quite measure up, for a given year’s cohort can usually show only a couple of young men who are able to lift the stone from the ground.

The oldest inhabitants of Nedervetil relate that Tomasasstäinä had already been an object of interest to confirmation-school youth even before their time. Moreover, they all explain that the stone derives its name from a man called Tomas, who lived quite near the church, namely at Måsabacka. This Tomas is said to have carried the stone the approximately 3–4 km-long distance from the church to its present location. If this is true, one may imagine that he rested several times along the way. Those who recount the connection between Tomas and the stone generally do not know when he lived. One person has, however, provided the information that Tomas was born around the year 1800.

— Walter Herrgård

Note. Approximately, the stone may be regarded as a right prism whose base is a triangle with sides of 56, 46, and 60 cm, and whose height is 28 cm. From these figures the stone’s volume is calculated to be about 34 dm³. Assuming a specific gravity of 2.7, the stone’s weight is approximately 92 kg.

Ei siinä ole mitään ihmettelemistä. Siinä suvussa on aina ollut isoja miehiä. Oletkos kuullut puhuttavan siitä Isosta Rönköstä, joka asui tuossa Rönkkölän talossa?

Nostokiven kalliolla oli vielä minun nuorena ollessani Ison Rönkön kantama kivi. Sen hän oli ottanut Lehtoniemen pellolta aamiaiselle tullessaan kainaloonsa, pudottanut Kaijanmäen tien varteen ja sanonut:
»Mies joka tuon nostaa maasta ylös, ei ole huono eikä vahva.» Siitä on sekin paikka saanut Nostokiven kallion nimen.

»Pyhäillat kisasivat sen kiven kanssa ja särkivät miehet sivujaan. Oli Puomilan paikalla asunut myös Iso Rönkkö ja hänestähän on Puomila nimensäkin saanut.»
»Siitäpä olisi hauska kuulla isännän kertovan», sanoin.
excerpt_en:
He settled comfortably into the rocking chair, carefully focused on lighting his cigar, and continued:

“You wonder why the younger shoots of the Rönkkö family in this village are so powerfully built. There is nothing to wonder about. That family has always had big men. Have you heard tell of Big Rönkkö, who lived there at the Rönkkölä farm?

He was a big man indeed. He worked as a blacksmith. An ordinary man used as his sledgehammer the hammer with which Big Rönkkö had forged. Even the shores of Rutakko rang out when he clanged away at his forging in the smithy.

On the rock of the lifting stone there was still, when I was young, a stone carried there by Big Rönkkö. He had taken it under his arm from the field at Lehtoniemi while coming in for breakfast, dropped it by the roadside at Kaijanmäki, and said:
‘The man who lifts that from the ground is neither poor nor weak.’

That is how the place, too, got its name, Nostokiven kallio [the Rock of the Lifting Stone].

Many a man tested his strength there to earn the reputation of a strong man. Taavetti of Rönkkölä, now deceased, managed to lift the stone. But when a folding knife was placed on top of it, even he could no longer raise it from the ground. At last Jussi of Lähdeniemi had a horse drag the stone into a mud pit.

‘Why did he get angry with that stone?’

‘On holy evenings men competed with that stone and smashed their sides against it. Big Rönkkö had also lived at the place called Puomila, and it is from him that Puomila got its name.’

‘That would be a fine thing to hear the master tell about,’ I said.”

URHEILIJALLE kirjoitti OSKARI NOUSIAINEN.
Kotiseutuni on erään pitäjän uloin kolkka karussa Suur- Savossa.Väkikiviä on vanhempaan aikaan ollut joka kylässä. Kangasniemessä on sellaisia ollut paljon — on kait vieläkin. Nuorena (23-vuotiaana v. 1823) kuollut talollinen Antti Nousiainen on pitäjän historian mukaan ollut kuuluisa voimamies, joka kävi salaa viskaamassa entisen väkikiven korkean kujan aidan yli kuin ei mitään. Se on myöskin todellinen sikäli, että se on kansan kertomuksissa kudottu arvoa ja kunnioitusta nauttineiden miesten nimen ympärille. excerpt_en:
**THE IDEAL MAN OF MY HOMELAND.**
Written for *Urheilijalle* by **Oskari Nousiainen**.

My homeland lies in the outermost corner of a parish in the barren region of **Suur-Savo**. In earlier times, lifting stones (*väkikivet*) existed in every village. In **Kangasniemi** there were many of them—and there probably still are. According to parish history, a farmer named **Antti Nousiainen**, who died young (at the age of 23 in 1823), was a renowned strongman who secretly went and tossed the former lifting stone over the tall fence of the manor avenue as if it were nothing.

Yet these popular recollections have a greater and deeper value. They gradually take shape as an outline of a male ideal. For of every strongman it has always also been said whether he was “handsome and fine-looking,” what his character was like, and so forth. Each region has its own folk ideal of manhood. It is also real in the sense that, in popular narratives, it is woven around the names of men who enjoyed esteem and respect. And this ideal man of my homeland would, by the standards of even the ancient world, be fit for the contest field—although of his deeds there now remain only fields cleared on barren slopes with their sturdy stone fences, and the lifting stones themselves, already overgrown with moss.

Tavallista kesäpäivän pyhätyötä oli kärryjen viskaaminen akselista pään ylitse. Siihen kyllä, jos kärryt olivat isot, ei joka mies kyennyt. Suutari-Vihtori yritti kerran ja väänsi itsensä pilalle, mutta monet raavaat ukot heittelivät kärryjä vain kerta toisensa perästä. Eheää miestä vaati väkikivenkin nosto, joka myös oli jokapyhäistä askartelua. Monen talon kartanolla oli komea väkikivi, jota sadat kourat olivat kuluttaneet ja yhä kuluttivat. Monesti vielä naisetkin olivat kivennostossa miesten kanssa kilpasilla. Jylhän naiset olivat oikein raikuja ihmisiä, puhumattakaan Rotmon tyttäristä. excerpt_en:
A common form of Sunday pastime on summer days was throwing carts by the axle up over one’s head. If the carts were large, not every man was capable of it. Suutari-Vihtori tried once and ruined himself, but many rugged old fellows hurled the carts again and again. Lifting the *väkikivi* likewise demanded a sound man, and it too was a regular Sunday occupation. In the yards of many farms there stood a fine *väkikivi*, worn smooth by hundreds of hands—and still being worn. Often even women competed with men in stone lifting. The women of Jylhä were truly formidable folk, not to mention the daughters of Rotmo.

But when Poras-äijä came to a group of men straining at a great *väkikivi*, he simply took it and threw it over the fence, saying:
— A man ought not to bother lifting a thing like that!

Old Poras-äijä was such a woodsman that he carried full tar barrels two at a time, holding them only by the bung holes with his finger hooks. Yet the master of the Mosala farm in the village of **Kaustinen** was in his day even more formidable. The whole district knew to speak of him, and even the powerful military commander of **Kokkola** rode out to see him, met him in the yard, and said:
— I have heard there are mighty men here … that one might put to the test.
— So it has been heard! Mosalainen merely replied.

A rare kind of court case.
The removal of “Mattilan mummo” to a museum gave rise to legal proceedings.

At the winter assizes soon to be held in Sysmä, a case of an unusual nature will be heard. A farmer, Tuomas Nyberg, from the village of Liikola, has summoned another farmer, Evert Peltola, also of Liikola, to court on the grounds that Peltola, at the request of Sysmän Sisu, had delivered to the Itä-Hämeen museo the so-called “Mattilan mummo,” a lifting stone formerly used in the village of Liikola, because it had been left to drift and fall into neglect. Members of the board of Sysmän Sisu have likewise been summoned to the assizes for the purpose of being heard.

The said “Mattilan mummo” is a round stone weighing 180 kg, the lifting of which has in the aforementioned village been regarded as a high demonstration of manliness.

excerpt_en:
The transport of “Mattilan Mummu” in Sysmä.

On the 14th of this month, the case brought by farmer J. Nyberg was for the second time heard before the Sysmän kihlakunnanoikeus against farmer E. Peltola, concerning the fact that in April of this year he had, without the plaintiff’s permission, removed and transported the lifting stone (nostokivi), the so-called “Mattilan Mummu,” which had been located by the roadside in the village of Liikola, to the village of Tikkala in the parish of Sysmä, from where the stone was further transported by another driver to the Itä-Hämeen museo.

In this case the defendant had also summoned to be heard the board of the V. and U. association Sysmän Sisu, which had initiated the transport, as was shown by a written statement submitted to the court on behalf of the association.

The court rendered the following decision in the matter: The district court, having examined the case, finds that the defendant E. Peltola, although believing himself entitled to do so, transported from the Jussila land owned by the plaintiff the stone known as Mattilan Mummu. The district court, relying on Chapter 16, Section 14, subsection 1 of the Penal Code, deems it proper to sentence the defendant for unlawful self-help to five day-fines, calculated at 15 marks per day, amounting to a fine of 75 marks, or, in default of payment, to be held for 10 days’ imprisonment, and to compensate the plaintiff’s costs in the amount of 700 marks. However, since the stone was no longer in the possession of Evert Peltola, the district court did not consider itself able to oblige the defendant to return mummu, and the claim in that respect therefore lapses.

Farmer Peltola is appealing the decision.

Pentti Niemi is the leading figure in the sporting life of Itä-Häme, a man who has borne both burden and heat in order to raise the standard of sport in the region. In that sense, Pentti Niemi has perhaps accomplished a greater day’s work than any other sportsman from Lahti. In Sysmä he has energetically promoted the construction of a sports field, and although obstacles have never been lacking—starting with “Mattilan mummu”—Niemi has, with Häme-like perseverance, resolved to carry the matter through to the end. Owing to Niemi’s efforts, Sysmän Sisu has indeed become one of the most vigorous rural sports clubs in our district.

excerpt_en:
“Mattilan Mummu” threatened with removal from the Hartola museum.

According to information we have received, farmer Juho Nyberg intends today to remove the so-called lifting stone (nostokivi) known as “Mattilan Mummu” from the Hartolan museo.

As the reader will recall, Mummu was donated to the museum by the V. and U. association Sysmän Sisu. However, since Nyberg has, to our knowledge, not notified the association concerned nor the museum board of his intention, such an action appears arbitrary.

«Mattilan Mummun** takaisin paluu Liikolaan tapahtui viime sunnuntaina.
Aikaisemmat hakuyritykset ja suunnitelmat keskeytyivät sen johdosta, että Museon johto pyysi neuvotella asiasta ensin maanviljelijä Juho Nybergin kanssa. Nyttemmin neuvottelut kuitenkin päättyivät siihen, että ikimuistoissa ollut nostokivi »Mattilan Mummu" oli luovutettava Jussilan emännäksi. V. ja U-seura Sisun puhemiesneuvosto katsoi tässä tapauksessa velvollisuudekseen kiven takaisinkuljetuksen, koska seuran taholta oli erehdytty Mummun poisviemiseen. Mummun takaisinpaluu tapahtui loistobiilillä ja Sisun puhemiehet syvästi nöyryytettynä käsissä pidellen veivät Mummun Juho Nybergin ja poikain kartanolle viime sunnuntaina.

“Mattilan Mummu” returned to Liikola last Sunday.

Earlier attempts to retrieve the stone and related plans were halted because the museum leadership requested that the matter first be negotiated with farmer Juho Nyberg. The negotiations have since concluded with the decision that the long-remembered lifting stone, “Mattilan Mummu,” was to be handed over to the mistress of the Jussila.

The presidium of the V. and U. association Sysmän Sisu considered it their duty in this case to arrange the stone’s return transport, as the association had erred in removing Mummu in the first place. The return took place by automobile, and the chairmen of Sisu—deeply humbled and carrying Mummu in their hands—delivered her to the estate of Juho Nyberg and his sons last Sunday in Liikola.

I. GEMENSKAP OCH MILJÖ

Före skriftskolsåldern kallas de t. ex. i Munsala »kvaddar» (ungtjäder av årets kull) eller »glopar», (Arv.N. Vö; J.A. S. Nä). De yngre pojkarna försöker i allmänhet inte tränga sig in i de äldres krets, men det finnes en del framfusiga, och till en sådan pojkvalp brukar man säga:»Kom inte hit, du har inte gått i skriftskolan!», »du är ännu inte torr bakom öronen» eller »gå hem och håll mamma i kjolen» (J.S. Nb; M.S. Tj). Det är inte att undra på, att en del pojkar försöker fjäska med skriftskolan för att tidigare få räkna sig till de äldre.

Det förekommer vissa slags »karlaprov», genom vilka det gäller att visa, att man lämnat barnaåren bakom sig och nu duger som fullgod karl. 1 ) I samband med skriftskolan övar sig pojkarna i olika slags styrkeprov, t. ex. att »lyfta sten» (D.I; A.A. Pe). De stenar, som därvid begagnas, kallas »skriftskolstenar» (M.H. Mb; K.G.A. La). En sådan sten, som skall lyftas upp i famnen, finnes invid kyrkomuren i Oravais. I Pedersöre finnes en dylik sten bakom klockstapeln vid kyrkan. Får man bara upp stenen från marken, så är provet klarat. Stundom gäller det att resa stenen i upprätt ställning. Ibland heter det, att en yngling inte får gifta sig eller räkna sig som fullvuxen, förrän han orkar lyfta stenen i höjd med knäna. Stundom får man lägga ett rep omkring stenen, som kan väga upp till 250 kg (J.R. Pe; M.H. Nb; M.S. Tj; N.R.Pu).

Stenen kan också vara försedd med järnband, ring eller krok. En sådan sten fanns före sekelskiftet på rådstugugården i Nykarleby. Den kallades »junttansten», och man använde den till att påla med. Det var särskilt »skriftskoleschacket» som övade sig flitigt i att resa upp den i stående ställning (E.E. Nb).

Under skriftskolstiden visar man på olika orter sitt mod och sina krafter genom att klättra upp i kyrktornet och sätta sig grensle på »tuppen», ställa sig att stå på tuppens rygg eller sätta en enriskrans på väderflöjeln. Ett annat manlighetsprov är, att de äldre pojkarna ute på rågåkern med lien gör ett »mågslag», d.v.s. slår en hel cirkel runt omkring sig själva (G.H. Vö).

Pojkarna visar även sina krafter genom att »brottas», »dra slätkäpp», »bryta arm», »lyfta stol», »dra handkavle», »dra fingerkrok», »lyfta kärrhjul» och »bära en tunna råg».
Det finnes i en del lekar knep, som kan göra, att man får en lätt, men ofta orättvis seger. Sådana knep är krokben eller »käringkrok», att vrida armen, slå mot munnen, magen eller under bältet eller att ha en träpinne inne i handen, då man drar fingerkrok med stropp (V.E.V.W. Si). Krokben är mestadels ett förbjudet knep i brottning. Det anses allmänt som fult, som en nödfallsutväg, oärligt och nesligt. En brottningskamp blir inte godkänd, om man sätter krokben för motståndaren, utan man måste börja på nytt. Åskådarna brukar också noggrant kontrollera, att inte någondera av kämparna sätter »käringkrok» för den andre (A.P. Si; N.R. Pu; J.S. Nb). Stundom är det dock tillåtet att lägga krokben för motståndaren (A.L. Or; I.R. Pe; R.R. Öv).

När en pojke gått genom skriftskolan, upphör lekarna. Han räknas nu som full karl och skall kunna utföra arbete som en hel karl. Han kallas för ungkarl och använder långbyxor. I början av seklet hände det ofta, att alla ogifta, yngre män efter genomgången skriftskola skulle bjudas på brännvin. Det var liksom ett manbarhetsprov. Sedan fick man börja gå på danser, »gå i ungdomen», som det kallades. Även föreningslivet lade band på ungdomarna. Men ännu förekommer det i den här åldern, att man slåss, tillfälligtvis eller med avsikt. Så t. ex. kan det hända att man på gungbacken råkar i delo om en flicka (N.R. Pu; 8.8. Si). Ofta ligger det kuntpatriotism bakom ett sådant slagsmål. Var och en håller pä sin hemgård och sin hemby och ger inte efter. Man utmanar varandra genom att kasta glåpord och skällsord till varandra. För det mesta är det nog äventyrslystnad, som ligger bakom slagsmålen (O.N. Nä; Y. G. Pe).

II. DEN MANLIGA UNGDOMENS IDROTTSLEKAR.

D LYFTNING OCH ANDRA STYRKEPROV.
Dl. Lyfta sten. Stenlyftning är ett vanligt styrkeprov, som oftast förekommer bland den manliga ungdomen. 1) Detta tillgår vanligast så, att man med båda händerna lyfter en stor sten, så att den ordentligt kommer upp från marken (Br). Ju större sten, desto starkare karl (Sb).
Man brukar ha speciella »lyftstenar» (lyftanstejnar), som det gäller att pröva styrkan på (Si). Dessa kan väga flere tiotal kg. Stundom, för att få
bättre tag, lägger man ett rep i tvenne öglor omkring stenen. Sedan gäller det att lyfta stenen det flesta antalet gånger (Py). I Terjärv finnes en lyftsten, som kallas »Risbackastein», bild 26. Den väger mellan 150—200 kg och har använts ungefär 200 år. Nu ligger den stödd på tvenne mindre stockar. För att det skall vara lättare att lyfta stenen, begagnar man en stark trädgren, mot vilken stenens vassa undre del vilar och vilken man tar tag i från vardera ändan. I forna tider var det en sed, påstår de gamla, att en man inte fick gifta sig, förrän han orkat lyfta stenen från marken (Tj). På kyrkbacken i Munsala finnes en sten, benämnd »ungkarlsstenen». Gossarna skulle lyfta den innan de ansågs som fullgoda ungkarlar. 2) En liknande sten, kallad »Stubbåkers grisen» (139 kg), finnes i Kantlax i Munsala. 3)
I Nedervetil kyrkoby finnes i Klockarbacken en sten, som kallas »Tomas’ sten» (Tåmasasstejne). Varje år prövar skriftskolepojkarna sina krafter på densamma. Den som orkar lyfta stenen från marken, betraktas av sina kamrater som fullvuxen, medan den r som inte mäktar med stenen, anses ha kommit för tidigt till skriftskolan. Stenen väger ungefär 92 kg och är mycket svår att få något tag på. Stenen har enligt hörsägen varit i bruk ett par hundra år. Det berättas, att en person vid namn Tomas, som bodde helt nära kyrkan, burit stenen från närheten av kyrkan ungefär 3/4 km till nuvarande plats, där den sedan dess fått ligga invid vägen. Efter denna person har stenen fått sitt namn (Nv).
På Åland i Björsby i Jomala finnes en lyftsten, i vilken årtalet 1783 är inhugget. Till formen är stenen äggrund (Jo), bild 27.
Ibland heter det, att den, som inte kan lyfta en lyftsten, inte räknas som riktig karl. Stundom lägger man ytterligare en eller flere stenar ovanpå, såsom vid »Nilsfafas lyftån» i Gästerby, Si. Ibland skall man lyfta stenen ända upp till bröstet (Si). Stundom har 15—16 års pojkar en egen sten och pojkarna i åldern 18—25 större stenar, som de lyfter (Nä). I vissa fall gäller det att lyfta stenen upp på axeln samt kasta den bakåt (Jo). Ibland gäller det att lyfta tyngsta stenen, ibland att kasta samma sten längst bakåt (Lf). Ibland skall stenen bäras en kortare eller längre vägsträcka. Den som gör det bäst, är starkast (Kn). Stenen skall först lyftas upp på axeln, sedan rakt upp i luften och kastas bakåt så långt som möjligt. Den som kastar längst är »välkast» (Nä).
Ibland lägger man sig på rygg på marken med armarna uppåtlyftade. Man fattar om stenen, lyfter den över huvudet och lägger den på magen. Härefter föres den samma väg tillbaka (Ha).

Mutta vain vaateorsien vaalijaksi ja tupakoreaksi ei nuorta naurusuista Liisaa Kinniään tuotu. Hän tiesi kyllä hyvin jo tullessaankin, että heti oli nuorikon miehen rinnalla käytävä raskaimpiinkin ulkotöihin ja tätä varten hän oli tuonut tullessaan omat tutut työkalunsakin: kassaran, sirpin, viikatteen, kirveen ja perukuokan.
Mutta kun suuri ja komea Marjaana, oikein kuuluisa työnraataja, tervametsien koloaja ja väkikivien nostaja samoihin aikoihin tuli Kyyjärven Nopolasta Perhon Jylhäseen miniäksi, oli hänellä vaateva-
rustusten, sekä huone- ja talouskalujen lisäksi mukanaan kaikki työkalut, mitä miehetkin tarvitsevat. Oli kolme kirvestä ja piilu neljäs, neljä viikatetta, sirppi ja kassari, perukuokka ja kytökuokka, talikko, kolme navaria, kolme höylää, kahdet kärryt ja reki sekä ketun ja sudenraudat.
excerpt_en:
But young, smiling Liisa Kinniä was not brought merely to tend the clothes poles and sit by the hearth. She knew very well already upon arriving that, alongside her husband, she would immediately have to take part in even the heaviest outdoor work, and for this purpose she had brought with her her own familiar tools: the kassara, sickle, scythe, axe, and the perukuokka.

But when the large and handsome Marjaana—truly famous as a tireless worker, a delver in tar forests, and a lifter of väkikivet—at about the same time came as a daughter-in-law from Nopola in Kyyjärvi to Jylhä in Perho, she brought with her—besides clothing and household furnishings—all the tools that men, too, require. There were three axes and a piilu as the fourth; four scythes; a sickle and a kassari; a perukuokka and a kytökuokka; a pitchfork; three augers; three planes; two carts and a sledge; as well as fox and wolf traps.

According to oral tradition, the site in question is a relatively recent one: a structure created as a display of strength, for which the designation väkikivet may be used. Similar accounts occur at least in old kihlakunta (judicial district) reports:

“The lower stone was lifted onto the small stones by a man named Kananen, and the upper and largest stone by Matti Pasanen of Vuohtomäki. Pasanen died a couple of years ago, perhaps in his seventies. As a motive for the stone arrangement, Raimo suggested a mutual display of strength between the men.”

excerpt_fi: Tuomas Rönkkö oli harvinaisen kookas ja voimakas mies. Hän oli kotoisin Sonkajärveltä ja tuli Ivaloon maantien tekoon. Tarina kertoo kuinka hän nosti ojasta valtavan kiven miesvoimin. Tapaus oli sen verran harvinainen, että kiveä alettiin kutsua Rönkönkiveksi. Voimamiehelle tapahtui kaikenlaista elämän varrella. Eräällä putkareissulla hän joutui painiotteluun miehen kanssa, joka osottautui hänen veljekseen.
excerpt_en:
Tuomas Rönkkö was an exceptionally large and strong man. He was originally from Sonkajärvi and came to Ivalo to work on the construction of the highway. The story tells how he lifted an enormous stone out of a ditch by sheer manpower. The incident was so remarkable that the stone came to be known as Rönkönkivi (“Rönkkö’s Stone”).

Many things befell the strongman over the course of his life. On one occasion, during a stint in jail, he became involved in a wrestling match with another man—who turned out to be his own brother.

excerpt_fi: Friman, joka Huoruutensa parhaat vuodet täällä toimi, on jättänyt pysyvän muistan savonrantalaisten mieliin. Pappina hän vakavuudella., mutta samalla ystävällisenä ja usein toverillisena toimitti tehtävänsä. Mutta erikoisesti kiertelevät laajemmaltikin kertomukset hänestä näiltä ajoilta voimamiehenä, joka milloin hevosenkenkiä veti suoraksi, milloin nosteli hevosia ja rekiä tiepuoleen, milloin näytteli punnuksilla ja väkikivillä voimannäytöksiä jne. Savonrannan keski-iän ja vanhemman polven ihmiset muistavat hyvin hänet.
excerpt_en:
Friman, who served here during the best years of his clerical career, has left a lasting memory in the minds of the people of Savonranta. As a pastor he carried out his duties with seriousness, yet at the same time in a friendly and often companionable manner.

In particular, however, stories circulated more widely about him in those days as a strongman: at times he would straighten horseshoes by pulling them, at times lift horses and sledges up onto the roadside, at times give demonstrations of strength with weights and väkikivet, and so forth. The middle-aged and older generations of Savonranta remember him well.

excerpt_fi:
VOIMAMIEHIÄ ON MONENLAISIA
Omalaatuisimpia nykyisin elävistä voimamiehistämme on eurajoke-
lainen Frans Wahlros, joka samalla on ikiliikkujan keksijä ja paljon muutakin. VVahlrosin nykyinen asuinpaikka on pienessä korpikylässä Eurajoen tien varrella, mutta kotoa häntä tapaa harvoin. Jos maakunnassa vain on joitakin »kissan ristiäisiä», niin kyllä VVahlros on myös siellä. Erikoisen maineensa voimamiehenä hän on hankkinut siten, että lyö vetoa suurten kivien, viljasäkkien ym. kantamisesta. Hän kuuluukin nostavan hartioilleen sadan kilon säkin aivan vaivattomasti ja vääntelevän sellaisia kiviä, joita ta-
valliset miehet eivät saa liikahf; maankaan.
excerpt_en:
STRONGMEN ARE OF MANY KINDS

One of the most peculiar among our presently living strongmen is Frans Wahlros of Eurajoki, who is at the same time the inventor of a perpetual-motion machine and much else besides. Wahlros’s current place of residence is in a small backwoods village along the Eurajoki road, but he is seldom found at home. If anywhere in the province there happens to be any sort of “cat’s christening” (a local gathering or festivity), Wahlros will be there as well.

His particular fame as a strongman he has acquired by making wagers on carrying large stones, sacks of grain, and the like. He is said to hoist a hundred-kilogram sack onto his shoulders quite effortlessly and to wrestle with stones that ordinary men cannot budge from the ground at all.

excerpt_fi: Kylän miekkoset olivat tietoisia Juhanan tulosta ja eikös vain heille johtunut koiruus mieleen ja niinpä miehet vierittivät keskelle tietä suurimman kiven minkä irti saivat. Juhana tuli aikanaan myös kiven luo, pysäytti ajokkinsa, katseli hetken kiveä ja astuen rattailta tuumiskeli: "Katsos kun ovat pikkupojat käyneet leikkimässä." Nappasi kiinni kiveen ja heilautti sen yli aidan. Heilautti siitä huolimatta, että se oli todella melkoinen pulteri. Oli ainakin se kivi, mitä isäni aikoinaan minulle näytteli ja kertoili tapahtuneesta. Kivennostelua kerrotaan Juhanan harjoittaneen myös Ostamon kujasilla. Siellä oli kuulema kylän miehillä kujasten vieressä voimankoijtoskivi ja ken sitä sai liikautettua, häntä pidettiin miehenmittaisena. Sattui sitten kerran Juhanalle Myllypellon matka ja Ostamon kujasia ajaessaan näki kiven, muisti sen tarkoituksen ja pysäytti jälleen ajokkinsa, astahti tielle ja kiven viereen. Koetteli sen painoa, koetteli toisenkin kerran ja niin nappasi koko miehisen voiman koetuskiven yli kujasten aidan
excerpt_en:
The village fellows were aware of Juhana’s arrival, and sure enough a bit of mischief came to mind; so the men rolled the largest stone they could loosen into the middle of the road. In due time Juhana also came upon the stone, stopped his conveyance, looked at it for a moment, and stepping down from the shafts remarked: “Well now, looks like the little boys have been playing.” He seized the stone and swung it over the fence—swung it despite the fact that it was truly a hefty lump. It was at least the very stone that my father once showed me and told me about, recounting what had happened.

Stone lifting is also said to have been practiced by Juhana along the lanes of Ostamo. There, it is said, the village men had a stone by the roadside as a test of strength, and whoever could move it was regarded as a man of full measure. It then happened once that Juhana was on his way to Myllypelto, and as he drove along the lanes of Ostamo he saw the stone, remembered its purpose, and once again stopped his conveyance, stepped onto the road and up to the stone. He tested its weight, tested it a second time, and then seized the entire manhood-testing stone and hurled it over the lane fence.

excerpt_fi: Kuuluisimpana Suupohjan entisajan voimamiehenä mainitaan Tohni-niminen mies. Hän on ottanut osaa Kyrön kirkon rakentamiseen. Jälkimaailmalle muistoksi vieritti hän kirkon muurille yksin kiven, jota ei kymmenen miestä jaksanut kuletella.
excerpt_en: The most famous strongman of earlier times in Suupohja is said to have been a man named Tohni. He took part in the construction of Kyrön kirkko. As a memorial for posterity, he single-handedly rolled onto the church wall a stone that ten men had not been able to transport.

excerpt_fi: Nimellisiä kiviä: Muukilaisten rajamerkiksi sanotaan Lehtimäellä noita vähäisillä kivijaloilla seisovia väkikiviä, joita ei tähän aikaan voida miehissäkään huiskuttaa. Valtarin mäellä kerrotaan olevan neljä yhdessä rivissä, joka käy erään peuranhaudoistaan tunnetun harjanteen poikki. Pylväiden väliä sanotaan olevan noin 150 askelta. Siitä pylväsrivistä kuuluu vielä poikkeavan toinen rivi mäkeä pitkin, mutta siinä on vaan kaksi pylvästä. Tässä esiintyvä Muukilaisnimi varmaankin vaan on paikallismuoto Munkkilaisnimestä, joka samoin kuin Nunnanimikin on ehtinyt saada myytillisen merkityksen rahvaan käsityksessä.
excerpt_en:
Named stones: In Lehtimäki, those väkikivet standing on small stone bases are said to serve as boundary markers of the Muukilaiset (“foreigners”), stones that even today cannot be tossed about by men. On Valtarin mäki, there are said to be four set in a single row crossing a ridge known for its pitfall traps for elk. The distance between the pillars is said to be about 150 paces. From this row of pillars another row is said to diverge along the hill, but that one has only two pillars.

The name Muukilainen occurring here is surely merely a local form of Munkkilainen (“monk”), which—like Nunnaniemi (“nun”)—has come to acquire a mythical significance in popular belief.

excerpt_fi: Nimellisiä kiviä: Siikajoessa on Gananderin mukaan kaksi kiveä Kiljonkivi ja Koljonkivi, joiden väliä, noin 100 aironvetoa, sanotaan Koljon suvannoksi. Kivet ovat tarinan tieten kahden kilpailevan jättiläisen Kiljon ja Koljon heittämiä.
excerpt_en: Named stones: In Siikajoki, according to Ganander, there are two stones called Kiljonkivi and Koljonkivi, the stretch of water between them—about one hundred oar-strokes—is said to be known as Koljon suvanto. According to the tale, the stones were thrown by two rival giants, Kiljo and Koljo.

excerpt_fi: Piirteitä Pohjois-Karjalaisista kansanhuveista ja ajanviettotavoista entisaikaan: Väkikivennosto oli myös suosittu kesäinen urheilu. Pihassa tai lähistöllä oli usein eri kokoisia kiviä vallanvasten väkikiviksi varattuja. Nämä kivet säilyivät välistä useamman sukupolven ajan omilla sopivasti valituilla paikoillaan esim. pellon pientarella. Jatkuvan harjoituksen kautta saavutettiin väkikivennostossa erinomaisia, myöhempää polvea ihmetyttäviä tuloksia. Kyllä muistaa näiden rivienkin kirjoittaja hämmästyksensä, kun hänelle näytettiin isoisänßä väkikivi. Poika ei ollut saanut sitä tuumaakaan nousemaan ja pojanpoika tuskin muuten kuin kankien avulla. Polvi heikkonee!
excerpt_en:
Features of North Karelian folk amusements and pastimes in former times:
Lifting väkikivi was also a popular summer sport. In the farmyard or nearby there were often stones of various sizes deliberately set aside specifically as väkikivet. These stones sometimes remained in their suitably chosen places—such as at the edge of a field—for several generations. Through continual practice, excellent results were achieved in väkikivennosto, feats that later generations would marvel at. Even the writer of these lines recalls his own astonishment when he was shown his grandfather’s väkikivi. The son had not managed to raise it even an inch, and the grandson scarcely at all except with the aid of levers. The generations grow weaker!

excerpt_fi: Kansan vanhoista voimisteluliikkeistä; sormikoukun, kissanhännän ja väkikartunvetämisestä sekä syli-, hartia- ja vyöpaininheittämisestä, hypyistä ja väkikivien nostamisista kantaa moni varomattomuutensa ja liiallisen rohkeutensa muistona vammoja vanhuutensa loppuun asti.
excerpt_en: Of old folk strength exercises: from finger-hook pulling (sormikoukku), cat’s-tail pulling (kissanhäntä), and väkikarttu pulling, as well as throws in bosom-, shoulder-, and belt-wrestling, jumps, and the lifting of väkikivet, many bear—through their own carelessness and excessive boldness—injuries as lasting reminders, carried with them to the very end of old age.

excerpt_fi: Voimistelun ja urheilun merkitys on moninainen: Sitä todistaa myöskin se nykyisen vanhemman polven nuoruudenaikainen tapa kokoontua yhteen nostelemaan „väkikiveä“, painimaan, vetämään köyttä tai juoksemaan leskistä
excerpt_en: The significance of physical exercise and sport is manifold: this is also demonstrated by the youthful custom of the present older generation of gathering together to lift väkikivi, to wrestle, to pull rope, or to run leskistä (traditional footraces).

excerpt_fi: Entisajan urheilua: lujat työmiehet kun saattoivat olla laajaltikin kuuluja ja samalla haluttuja. Että työkilpa on kuulunut tavalla tai toisella esivanhempiemme "huvitteluun" jo muinaissuomalaisena aikana, siitä ei liene epäilystä. — Nykyään tämä kilpailutapa kuulunee jo muistojen joukkoon. Voitaisiin näet puhua mitä moninaisimmista otteluista, urheilupeleistä ja kilpaleikcistä, kuten kiekonlyönti, sylipaini, väkikiven nosto, kissanhäntä, niskanuora y.m., joista jo kirjallisiakin tietoja on olemassa ainakin 1700--luvulla, mutta vaikeus on vain siinä, tutkimus kun on vasta alullaan, mitä voi laskea "muinaissuomalaisten" harjoittamiksi, mitä ei. Ettei erilaisista urheilutavoista ole ollut puutetta, saattaa arvata jo siitä, että urheilu- ja leikkityyppejä on laskettu löytyvän Suomessa noin 500. Vienan-karjalaisilta, aunukselaisilta, inkeriläisiltä ja vepsäläisiltä tehtyjen muistiinpanojen nojalla saattaisi ehkä jokunen urheiluleikki palautua n.s. yhteissuomalaiselle ajalle asti, mutta niistä ei vielä tällä kertaa uskalleta lausua mitään varmaa.
excerpt_en:
Sport in former times: strong working men could become widely renowned and at the same time much sought after. That labor competition, in one form or another, belonged to the “amusements” of our forefathers already in ancient Finnish times can hardly be doubted. Today, however, this form of competition seems to belong to the realm of memory.

One could speak of a great variety of contests, sports, and competitive games—such as discus throwing (kiekonlyönti), bosom wrestling (sylipaini), lifting the väkikivi, cat’s tail (kissanhäntä), neck-rope (niskanuora), and so forth—about which written information already exists at least from the 18th century. The difficulty lies only in the fact that research is still in its early stages as to what may be counted as practices of the “ancient Finns” and what may not.

That there was no shortage of different forms of sport may be inferred already from the fact that some 500 types of sports and games are said to be found in Finland. On the basis of records made among the Vienan Karjala (White Sea Karelia), the Aunus (Olonets), the Inkeri (Ingrians), and the Vepsä (Vepsians), it might be possible that some sporting games could be traced back as far as the so-called Common-Finnic period; but for the time being, nothing certain can yet be stated about this.

excerpt_fi: Hiukan sunnuntain vietosta ja pesäpallopelistä kansallispelinä.: Jo entisaikaan on esi-isillä ollut omat sunnuntai-ilonsa ja tapansa. Kuitenkaan ei ole vielä siihen aikaan ollut mitään yhteistä ilo- tai leikkitapaa yli koko maan, vaan tavallista on ollut, että sunnuntaisin on kokoonnuttu määrättyihin paikkoihin iloa pitämään, itsekullakin paikkakunnalla omalla tavallaan. Useissa paikoin on ollut pallonlyönti yleisin, toisissa visakiekko tai joku kapulan heitto, ja siinä sivulla on ollut väkikiven nostot, sylipainit ja monet muut urheilulliset pelit ja leikit, joissa on kylänkin kunniaa puolustettu.
excerpt_en:
A little about Sunday observance and the game of pesäpallo as a national sport:
Already in former times our forefathers had their own Sunday pleasures and customs. Yet at that time there was no single shared form of amusement or play across the entire country; rather, it was customary on Sundays to gather at designated places to enjoy oneself, each locality in its own way. In many places ball striking was the most common pastime; elsewhere it was throwing a wooden discus (visakiekko) or some form of club throwing. Alongside these there were lifts of the väkikivi, bosom wrestling (sylipaini), and many other athletic games and pastimes, in which the honor of the village itself was also defended.

excerpt_fi:
Kaartilainen: Koko Hoskavaaran kylän miehistä oli Mikko pisin ja sitäpaitsi vahvin. Tämä Mikon voimain runsaus tuli näkyviin „kissan hännän" ja sormikoukun vedossa, sekä kiven nostossa ja sylipainissa. Ja että lastu-Mikko niissä voiton vie tiedettiin koko pitäjässä. Miehet olivat kokoontuneet pihamaalle „väkikiveä" nostamaan. Se oli suuri kivi eikä noussut koholle keltään.
— No, lastu-Mikko, tahi kaartilainenhan sinä olet, tuleppas ja kohota kivi.
— Tuommoisen mukulan nosto on leikkiä ettei oikein viitsisi, mutta voihan tuota koettaa, sanoi Mikko ja ähkien ja puhkuen känysi kiven kimpussa, joka tosin kohosikin ylös.
excerpt_en:
Kaartilainen: Of all the men in the village of Hoskavaara, Mikko was the tallest and, moreover, the strongest. The abundance of Mikko’s strength showed itself in pulling the “cat’s tail” (kissanhäntä) and the finger hook (sormikoukku), as well as in stone lifting and bosom wrestling (sylipaini). And that Lastu-Mikko would carry off the victory in these was known throughout the entire parish.

The men had gathered in the farmyard to lift the väkikivi. It was a large stone and would not rise for anyone.

— Well then, Lastu-Mikko—or you’re the Guardsman (kaartilainen), after all—come and raise the stone.

— Lifting such a lump is child’s play, hardly worth the effort, but one can try, said Mikko, and grunting and snorting he wrestled with the stone, which indeed did rise up.

excerpt_fi: Ja kaikkia noita ominaisuuksia osasi Kalle käyttää. Vain väkikiven nostossa ja väkikartun vedossa muutamat kylän suurimmat miehet hänet voittivat, eivät muussa, vaikka otteluita järjestettiin talven mittaan joskus hyvinkin paljon. Sillä tuo näennäisesti heiveröinen, kalpeaposkinen mies sai hyvin helposti houkutelluksi jonkun oudon voimamiehen kanssaan sylipainin heittoon, joka oli oikein Kallen erikoisala.
excerpt_en: And all of these qualities Kalle knew how to use. Only in lifting the väkikivi and in pulling the väkikarttu was he defeated by a few of the largest men in the village—never in anything else—even though matches were sometimes arranged in great numbers over the course of the winter. For this seemingly frail, pale-cheeked man could very easily entice some unfamiliar strongman into a bout of bosom wrestling (sylipaini), which was truly Kalle’s particular specialty.

excerpt_fi:
Urheiluharrastuksista: Joloskylän n.-s:n talolla 23/ 13 piti Ewil Leskelä seuraawan puheen: Monesti olemme kuulleet wanhempien miesten hehkuwin, innostunein mielin kertoelewan niistä walwotuista waloisista kesäöistä, jotka louolle roihuwien, sawuawien terwahautojen ääressä kirppaa (katajainen 4 tuumaa ytkä karttu jota koiwukepillä maalikiwen luota lyötiin) ja palloa lyöden sekä painien ja terwatynnyreitä ja wäkikiwiä nostellen wietettiin. Kuinka monesti olemme kuulleet wanhojen miesten kiistelewän sitä, ken pallo-
silla ja kirpalla ollessa oli maalin tai „ämmä-kiwen" paras suojelija, ken rskin painissa, tai wäkikiwen ja hyppypölkyn nostossa, ken käsikartun wedossa tai kiwen haitossa paras oli. Ei sillä ettei nykyään paikkkannaltamme löytyisi aineksia joisa woitaisiin kehittää kykyjä jotka woisiwat näyttää kuntoaan waikka Olyrbian kisoissa, sillä sitä todistaa täystäisen terwa-„puolikon" kanto takkewitassa pitkiä rappusia myölen kirken harjalle, seki wakikiwen nostot ja erään pojan juoksu 1 km. maikalla täällä pidetyissä juoksukilpailuissa w. 1910.
excerpt_en:
On sporting pursuits: At the N.-S. farm in Joloskylä on 23/13, Ewil Leskelä delivered the following address:

“Many times we have heard older men, with glowing enthusiasm, recount those guarded, luminous summer nights that were spent by blazing, smoking tar pits—playing kirppa (a juniper stick about four inches thick, struck with a birch bat from the marker stone), striking the ball, wrestling, and lifting tar barrels and väkikivi. How often we have heard old men argue over who, when playing ball and kirppa, was the best defender of the goal or the ‘ämmä-kivi’ (mother stone); who was the best in wrestling, or in lifting the väkikivi and the jumping log; who excelled in pulling the hand club (käsikarttu) or in stone throwing.

Not that nowadays our locality would lack material from which abilities could be developed that might show their mettle even at the Olympic Games; this is proven by the carrying of a full tar ‘half-barrel’ in a back-basket up long stairways to the ridge of the church, likewise by väkikivi lifting, and by a certain boy’s run over a distance of one kilometer in the running competitions held here in the year 1910.”

excerpt_fi: Nurmeksen maalais-yhdistyksen kilpailuhuwit: Paras ampuja ampui 15 senttimeetriä, 54 naulan painoista nostettiin 50 kertaa, wäkikiwen nostossa kohosi 47 leiwiskää, 54 sekunnissa juostiin 340 meetriä, paras aitumus ponnahti 63 tuumaa. Nämä jo muita mainitsematta todistawat, että: „wiel' on woimaa Suomessa, miehiä ja miehuutta". Naisillakin oli kilpailunsa. Heidät sidottiin liinalla sokoksi ja annettiin sitten käteen sakset, joilla heidän tuli leikata poikki joku wartaasta riippuwa lanka, johon woitto oli ripustettu. Sitä oli kyllä hupainen katsoa, mutta samalla johtui siitä myöskin mieleen naisen asema entisinä ja nykyisinä päiwinä. Naista näet johdattanee wain yhä sokea sallimus. Sitä pitää wain mennä teppuroida etehen päin, sattui sitte päämaaliin tahi ei. Kun miesten pitää tarkistaa järkensä, silmänsä ja kaikki muut woimansa, niin täytyy naisen waan säkkipäänä töllöttää. Ampumisesta: 1:sen palk., 20 mk., Antti Koukkari, 15 sentim., 2:sen 12 mk., Juho Kiiskinen, 17 sentim., 3:nen 8 mk., kirjuri K. E. Turunen, 20 sentim., ja 4:nen, 4 mk., yliopp. K. Relander 24 sentim. Wäkikiwen nostosta: 1:sen palk., 1 mk. 50 p., Pekka Tolonen, nosti 47 L8, 2:sen, 1 mk., Olli Moilanen, nosti 47 L2, ja 3:nen, 50 p., Taawi Tinnonen, nosti 44 L8. Painojen nostosta: 1:sen palk., 1 mk. 50 p., Olli Tolwanen, nosti 54 [naulaa] 50 kertaa, 2:sen, 1 mk., Pekka Newalainen, nosti saman 26 kert., ja 3:nen, 50 p., Wille Piironen, nosti saman 13 kert. Korkeushypystä: 1:sen palk., 1 mk. 50 p. F. Sikanen, hyppäsi 63 tuum., 2:sen, 1 mk., A. Rantanen, hyppäsi 60 tuum., ja 3:nen, 50 p., M. Puoskari. aiwan nuori, hyppäsi 45 tuum. Kuulan heitosta: 1:sen palk., 1 mk. 50 p., Pekka Newalainen, heitti 16 [naulan] pain. kuulan 36 jalk., 2:sen, 1 mk., Olli Tolwanen, heitti saman 32 jalk., ja 3:nen, 50 p., Olli Eskelinen, heitti saman 32 jalk. Pituushypystä: 1:sen, 1 mk., T. Sikanen, hyppäsi 14½ jalk., ja 3:nen, 50 p., P. Newalainen, hyppäsi 14 jalk.

excerpt_en:
Sport and physical exercise have been practiced in Kaustinen since ancient times. Sporting implements included väkikivet (lifting stones), kissanhäntä (“cat’s tail”), cart wheels, and the like. In addition, competitions were held in finger-hook pulling, throws in sylipaini (bosom wrestling), and running.

A väkikivi was a heavy stone block that a man was required to lift. The most famous of these was the “rye-bread stone,” which only the men of rye bread—that is, the strongest—could lift. Kissanhäntä was usually pulled from a stick, most often with one hand; the winner was the man in whose grip the stick finally remained. Cart wheels were thrown up to the chest or over the head; the strongest performed this with one hand. Competitions arose wherever several men happened to gather, but they were also organized at weddings and christenings, often featuring short-distance running.

There were strongmen whose deeds the present generation listens to as legend. Even today stories are told of “Mosalan Äijä”—also called “Iso Mosalainen”—who, while delivering tar in Kokkola, gave a strongman’s answer when gentlemen asked about the quality of the tar. Mosalainen promised to show them. He went to his tar load, opened the bung of a “large barrel,” put his middle finger through the hole, and by that carried the barrel up the high stairs into the gentlemen’s room. The gentlemen bought the tar without further ado and in addition offered the strongman a couple of drinks. Once, while at a market, Mosalainen traded horses and made a good bargain—so he lifted the horse up onto the loft of the stable. Others later tried to undo the deal, but could not get the horse down from the loft, even though Mosalainen offered to cancel the bargain.

Poukka Eljas was also a strongman, a famed sylipaini thrower and a fearsome runner. Likewise remembered are Iso Matti, Paksu Äijä, and others, each credited with a variety of feats of strength. It is said that Finnin Lassi lifted the rye-bread stone—and with fifteen “wet roach fish” placed on top.

It is true that the men mentioned above were larger and stronger than average. Especially Mosalan Äijä, who was a veritable giant in bodily build. Conditions of sport remained in this state quite late. Only during the last two decades did sport begin to assume its modern forms under the influence of youth associations. Thus the first summer athletic competitions were organized in connection with the summer festival of the youth-association district of Lappajärvi, at the so-called Eevanniemi, in 1905. Prior to that, winter ski competitions had already been arranged, the first at Köyhäjoki.

The first notable skiing competitions in Northern Finland were held as early as ten years before the first Oulun Hiihto. In 1879, skiing competitions were organized in Tyrnävä, about which only very little information has so far been obtained. A contemporary newspaper notice does state that on March 23, 1879, “competitive ski races” were held in Tyrnävä, with about 70 participants, and that prizes were awarded to the four best competitors: 3 marks to the first, 2 marks to the second, and 1 mark each to the next two.

However, the notice does not mention who won the competition or who the other prize recipients were, except that among the four best there was also one young woman. Men and women thus appear to have competed as equals in the same class.

The competition was won by a then well-known local athlete and väkikivi lifter, Antti Ollila, whose feats in lifting the väkikivi have left behind a local saying: “Mielii ja mielii niinkuin Ollilan Antilla” (“to keep trying and trying, like Antti Ollila”). Second place went to a man from Alatemmes known as “Susi-Suutari” (“Wolf the Cobbler”), whose real name is not remembered, as it was seldom used.

The narrator could not recall the recipients of the third and fourth prizes, but one of them was in any case a woman. The competitions were apparently organized by Härkönen, who at the time was the elementary school teacher of the Tyrnävä church village.

Paavo was not a sulking recluse living in isolation, as one might have assumed from his looks, but a true man of pursuits. He had more acquaintances than many a more handsome fellow, for everyone knew that whatever cause Paavo took upon himself, nothing would interrupt it except death or typhoid fever. Yet Paavo did not set out to pursue all manner of things at once. One thing at a time, and with determination—that was his order of work.

In his youthful years, when others were looking for a life partner, Paavo had taken up the pursuit of lifting väkikivi. It did not last many years, but it held him so completely in its grip that he did not even glance toward the womenfolk. During those years Paavo’s attention was turned toward the men who appeared the strongest, and they had to be utterly indifferent to the magnitude of their own strength if they refused to take part in lifting the väkikivi.

It measured 14 meters in length and 10 meters in width, a mound built of stones that a man could lift, whose base consisted of a roughly circular stone setting constructed of väkikivet.

North Karelian sporting practices of former times: 4. Lifting the väkikivi.
In olden days, the strongest man was the one who could raise the largest stone from the ground up to his body. Lifting the väkikivi—as it was called—was the principal test of strength for young men. It was practiced especially on holy evenings, when young men gathered together at certain places. For the sake of honor, some exerted themselves so much that they ended up crippled for life. From Hyrynsalmi:
For example, the long-bearded “Baron of Parkano,” Gustaf Wrede, known throughout the country, once served here as a regional forest officer. He was appointed forest master here, if I recall correctly, in the year 1883. From here he moved to Parkano some fifty years ago. He became known here for his integrity and modesty. The baron often wore a strangely cut homespun outfit, and his behavior was somewhat out of the ordinary, marked by whims and playful pranks. He wrestled, pulled the finger hook, and lifted väkikivi together with farmhands and log drivers. He was always good-humored and friendly.

From the novel Onnen vaiheet:

Strength began to be tested. Wrestling bouts were thrown, kissanhäntä and väkikarttu were pulled, and väkikivi was lifted. Risto of Rossi defeated the others, except for Hiski and Jukka, who did not take part in the trials. Risto had never beaten Jukka. It was said that he deliberately always left the victory to his friend. Jukka did not feel inclined to test his strength together with the others.

“Since I defeat Risto and he defeats you, you surely know even without testing who is the strongest,” he said.

As a sports apostle in Lapland:
In many other places the interest in sport is altogether heartening, but the entire well-populated stretch of the Ounasjoki, most of the Tornionjokilaakso, and many regions along the Kemijoki still live in darkness in this respect. Old men do recount that in their youth, on holy days, men would lift väkikivi, strike the ball, and at times even engage in wrestling. The most popular form of wrestling seems to have been collar wrestling, in which one grips the opponent by the waistband and swings his boots skyward.

In the tar-burning regions it used to be the custom among barrel-makers to compete in who could jump into the greatest number of barrels. The barrels were set in a row, the jumper stood in the first and then leapt from barrel to barrel—up to twelve barrels in all.

As winter pastimes, people pulled the finger hook (sormikoukku), the cat’s tail (kissanhäntä), and the neck strap (niskanauha), and sometimes wrestled as well. But nowadays it was widely lamented that young people would rather sit at cards or keep company with strong drink than give themselves over to innocent competitions.

excerpt_en:
On my travels I happened upon a certain homestead that was said to be old—and there was ample evidence to support that claim. As soon as I arrived at the yard, something of great age caught my eye. The homestead was large, with altogether some ten residential buildings. But what was remarkable was this: not a single building was roofed with any material other than birch bark. Perhaps a charcoal shed standing farther out from the yard was roofed with shingles, but no others could be seen.

I hurried to a chest in which old papers had been gathered for safekeeping. The receipts were made of stout paper, consisting of several sheets, but a plain Finn could make out little more than the year—1788 on the oldest preserved—and the payer’s name, Pehr, by which Pekka was meant. Then we examined all the storage chests, and there was much there that recalled times past, and not all the implements could even be understood as to what they had been used for.

As we wandered from one granary to another, the master of the house urged me to lift a certain stone lying by the roadside. I saw, from the fact that it had been placed upon small stones, that others too had tried it, and I could not resist attempting it myself. “This will not rise for me—does it rise for anyone else?” I said, when the stone would not budge. “It does rise for some. But it is said that the old men of this house once hurled it, by sheer arm strength, from the bottom of a deep pit, and according to what is heard they were supposed to have said: ‘There is a väkikivi for the men of generations to come.’”
“Well then, perhaps two men threw it.”
“No—alone.”
“Well, perhaps they had grown so strong from turning stony fields,” I conceded.

Folk festivities in Nurmes were held on the market town field on August 25. The festivities were organized by the Nurmes Rural Association and differed from ordinary folk amusements in that good ploughmen, ditch diggers, and handicraft makers were also rewarded. Only after some time did the smaller prize competitions begin—in rowing, running, jumping, lifting the väkikivi and weights, and in shot putting.

The peasants are altogether unaccustomed to running and jumping, and nothing particularly outstanding is to be expected from them in these events; but as regards the three competitions last mentioned, the people of Nurmes demonstrated that they still retain the sound strength of their forefathers and need not be ashamed to enter trials of strength with anyone, on any occasion whatsoever.

excerpt_en:
In a newspaper intended to deal with matters concerning Liminka, it can hardly be considered inappropriate to recall a certain master of olden times, who lived in the early and middle parts of the last century and died some fifty years ago. That man was the farmer Erkki Sunila of Liminka, of whom much was spoken in his own day and who is still often mentioned and remembered even now. Erkki Sunila owned at various times the farms of Sunila, Ursala, and Jussila, and perhaps others as well; thus the holding was large, comprising about several manttaali, which was truly a considerable amount under the control of a single man here in the North.

“Old Man Sunila,” by which name he was almost universally known and is still known today, was an excellent farmer, an energetic director of labor, and in every respect a suitable and exemplary master of a large estate. His manner of organizing work was first-rate and was carried out for the most part in the spirit of competition. Lifting the väkikivi, pulling the väkikarttu, lifting the näppipölkky, and the like, as well as striking the ball, delighted him greatly. On Sunday evenings his own men and the men of the village were allowed to strike the ball in Sunila’s large yard for two or three hours, during which the old man watched the play the entire time and took pleasure in it. When the appointed time came, he would say, “Well now, well now, now we stop,” and then it did indeed end, no matter at what stage the game might have been left.

Kylän nuoria miehiä kokoontui tapansa mukaan sunnuntain iltapuolella kisailemaan Kaipion talon tanhualle. Lyötiin kiekkoa, nosteltiin sylin täyteisiä väkikiviä, kiisteltiin voimista. Ja kun tähän kyllästyttiin, haettiin kartanolta kärrynpyörät miesjoukkoon.
Ainoastaan jotkut harvat jaksoivat heittää raskaasti raudoitetut työkärryn pyörät päänsä yli.
— Kehnoja miehiä! ylvästelivät nämä voiman miehet ja vetäytyivät eri sakkiin, ikäänkuin häveten kuulua heikkojen joukkoon.
— Kyllä Mattikin pyörät päänsä yli heittää, väitti muudan poikanulikka heikkojen joukosta. Pyörät kohoavat hitaasti — hitaasti. Polvet ja käsivarret vapisevat, tummat ohimosuonet tuskanpunaisilla kasvoilla pullistuvat ja yhä useampi hikihelmi vierähtää otsalle. Vaistomaisesti taipuu oman puolueen miesten ruumiit taaksepäin Matin mukaan. Mutta vastapuolueen miehet kumartuvat raskaasti eteenpäin, ikäänkuin siten lisätäkseen kiviä kuorman päälle. Jo on akseli silmien tasalla, paljaitten käsivarsien jänteet pingoittuvat, silmät sulkeutuvat . . . jännittävä odotus, henkeä pidätellen . . . ratkaiseva ponnistunut . . . jymähdys . . .
Korkeimmillaan ollessa putosi akseli pyöräin koko painolla Matin rinnan päälle ja kaasi hänet allensa tanhualle. Ei kukaan miehistä liikkunut paikaltaan. Mutta Marjaana juoksi kaatuneen luo, kohotti hänen verta vuotavan päänsä syliinsä ja huusi hänen nimeänsä. Vaan kun ei
saanut vastausta, hän pyörtyneenä hervahti Matin rikkoutuneen rinnan yli.
excerpt_en:
Only a few could manage to throw the heavily iron-rimmed work-cart wheels over their heads.

“Pathetic men!” boasted these men of strength, withdrawing into a separate group, as if ashamed to be counted among the weak.

“Why, Matti can throw the wheels over his head too,” claimed a certain lad from among the weaker group. The wheels rise slowly—slowly. Knees and forearms tremble, the dark veins at the temples swell on pain-reddened faces, and ever more beads of sweat roll down onto the brow. Instinctively the bodies of the men on his own side lean backward along with Matti. But the men of the opposing side bend heavily forward, as if to add stones to the load. The axle is already at eye level; the tendons of the bare arms strain tight; the eyes close… a tense waiting, breath held… the decisive exertion… a crash…

At its highest point the axle fell with the full weight of the wheels onto Matti’s chest and crushed him beneath it onto the yard. None of the men moved from where they stood. But Marjaana ran to the fallen man, lifted his bleeding head into her lap, and called his name. When she received no answer, she collapsed in a faint across Matti’s shattered chest.

Loppui sitten tuo mierolaisen iloton elämä, kun hän pääsi hewospojaksi muutamaan isoon taloon ja ja sitten rippikoulun käytyään wakinaiseksi wuosirengiksi. Silloithan oli taas elämä huotettomampaa ja oppi kunnolliseksi työmieheksi. Hänestä kehittyi rotewa ja hartiakas nuorukainen. Wahwimpia hän
oli wäkikiwen nostossa ja painin lyönnissä. Nuo muistot ne saiwat tuon raihnaisen Aapon wielä nytkin innostumaan.
excerpt_en: All the other folk were already asleep in the large main room of Kivelä, but Ruoti-Aappo was still awake. That bleak life of a drifter finally came to an end when he became a stable boy at a large farm and, after completing confirmation school, a permanent hired hand for the year. Then life was easier again, and he learned to become a proper working man. He developed into a sturdy, broad-shouldered youth. He was strongest in lifting the väkikivi and in the blows of wrestling. Those memories were what even now stirred the feeble Aappo to renewed enthusiasm.

excerpt_fi: Enson tehtaitten kymmenennet kesäurheilukilpailut suoritettiin viime lauantaina ja sunnuntaina Enson urheilukentällä. Nämät kisat ovat samalla olleet ikäänkuin perhejuhlia, joihin vanhan suomalaisen tavan mukaan Enson väki on tälle kentällä kokoontunut, kuten muinoin maassamme oli tapana kylänväen, niin vanhojen kuin nuorienkin, aina sunnuntaisin kokoontua kylänraitille kiekkoa lyömään ja väkikiveä nostamaan. Ne ovat samalla antaneet meille sen tunteen, että olemme saman kylän väkeä, yhtä perhettä, Enso-Gutzeitin joukkoa. Me saamme olla ylpeät siitä, että kilpailumme, jotka olivat laadussaan ensimmäiset maassamme, ovat herättäneet huomiota muuallakin ja on niitä meidän esimerkkimme mukaan ryhdytty järjestämään kautta koko maan eri teollisuusseuduille.
excerpt_en:
The tenth summer athletic competitions of the Enso-Gutzeit works were held last Saturday and Sunday at the Enso sports field. These competitions have at the same time been, as it were, family celebrations, to which—following the old Finnish custom—the people of Enso have gathered on this field, just as in former times in our country it was customary for the villagers, both old and young alike, to gather every Sunday on the village street to throw the discus and lift the väkikivi.

They have likewise given us the feeling that we are people of the same village, one family—the Enso-Gutzeit community. We may be proud that our competitions, which were the first of their kind in our country, have attracted attention elsewhere as well, and that following our example they have begun to be organized throughout the country in various industrial districts.

The office of Kinnunen was entrusted in 1887 to Juho Friman, who was born on 30 July 1862 and is today the vicar of the rural parish of Viipuri, celebrating his 75th birthday at about the same time as Savonranta. He served in Savonranta until 1901, thus for 14 years, being absent only for a few months in 1895, during which time Aleksanteri Vehniäinen, born 28 February 1869 and now the vicar of Vahviala, acted as deputy vicar.

Friman, who spent the best years of his youth serving here, has left a lasting memory in the minds of the people of Savonranta. As a pastor he carried out his duties with seriousness, yet at the same time in a friendly and often companionable manner. But in particular, stories circulated widely from those days about him as a strongman: at times he would straighten horseshoes by pulling them, at times lift horses and sledges up onto the roadside, at times give demonstrations of strength with weights and väkikivet, and so forth. The middle-aged and older generations of Savonranta remember him well.

excerpt_en:
In the backwoods villages of Raja-Karjala, one can still today hear grey-haired elders boast proudly of how, in their lineage, there once was a man whom none of the village men could defeat in pulling the väkikarttu or the kissanhäntä. Others had been the most accomplished in lifting the väkikivi, in discus throwing, or in pole vaulting; some in wrestling, in knocking down the log, and so forth.

In former times it never even occurred to young men to spend their time in drunkenness and the like; rather, each sought, according to his ability, to pass the time in the competitions mentioned above and to improve himself. In winter, people would gather in large numbers at some house, where evenings passed pleasantly in the measuring of strength, the telling of tales, the posing of riddles, the reciting of proverbs, and the echoing of songs from the Kalevala.

From these ways of life of our forefathers we can clearly see how physical exercise can restrain even the roughest nature from selfish passions. Therefore, more gymnastics and sport for our youth! For the development of body and mind is among the highest ideals of life, for which it is worth everyone’s while to work.

excerpt_en:
PEKKA KORPELA TALKS PLEASANTLY ABOUT THE SPORTS YEARS OF THE PAST.

Knowing that the merchant Pekka Komonen (Korpela) of Tenkalahti is familiar with many engaging details about the old sporting life of Käkisalmi and its surroundings—and that Komonen has a knack for presenting matters in a golden light of humor—Käkisalmen Sanomat interviewed him yesterday, among others.

Half a century ago, nothing was known of sport as such; everything that pointed toward sport was a matter of feats of strength. The first proper athletic competitions in Käkisalmi were held in connection with the city’s 600th anniversary celebrations on June 28, 1894, at the Old Castle. Before that, however, the locality had been home to strongmen such as Juho Vuohelainen of Vuohensalo and Juho Komonen of Tenkalahti, the interviewer’s grandfather.

The latter weighed about seven pud, crossed his eyes with a three-pud weight and then threw it onto the cellar roof, carried 308 kilograms on his back, and was otherwise such a brute that there were scarcely enough men who could get a hold of him to do him any harm. Once in Vuohensalo he carried four men at the same time up a steep sandy embankment, and during the period of the land partition (isojako) at Ostamo he lifted from the ground the so-called väkikivi and threw it over a fence—whereas no one else had been able to move that stone at all by sheer arm strength.
